topic: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
parentTitle: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
title: DBT and distress tolerance skills
blurb: Describe the four DBT skill modules and coach someone through an urge to self-harm using distress tolerance skills and a safety plan.
question: Chloe, 24, has emotionally unstable personality disorder and is in a DBT programme. At 2 am on the ward she tells you she has an overwhelming urge to cut. She is pacing and breathing fast. How should the nurse help?

teach.body: DBT, developed by Marsha Linehan, combines CBT-style change strategies with acceptance. 'Dialectical' means holding two truths at once: 'I accept myself as I am' AND 'I need to change'. It is designed for people with intense emotions, especially those who self-harm. A comprehensive programme includes individual therapy, group skills training and phone coaching. Plain English: learn to accept the wave of emotion, and learn skills to ride it out without making things worse.

teach.caption: Mindfulness underpins all four. Distress tolerance is for surviving a crisis without making it worse.

teach.h: Who NICE says to consider for DBT
head: Group
Guidance
rows: Women with BPD where reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority
Young people with frequent self-harm and significant emotional dysregulation
Do not withhold psychological help because of diagnosis, age or substance use (NG225 1.11.9)
teach.caption: NG225 1.11.10: do not offer drug treatment as a specific intervention to reduce self-harm.

letters.word: Temperature: cold water on the face
Paced breathing: breathe out slower than in

teach.caption: Used when emotion is so high that thinking skills cannot work yet. Check physical health before cold-water or exercise skills.

steps.label: Notice and name it
steps.sub: 'I have an urge; it will peak and pass'

steps.label: Review
steps.sub: Chain analysis next day with therapist

teach.caption: Urges rise, peak and fall like a wave: the aim is to get through the peak without acting.

items: Triggers and warning signs of rising distress or crisis.
Personal coping strategies, with ways round any barriers.
People and places that help distract; family or friends who can support.
Mental health service contacts, including out of hours and emergency numbers.
Making the environment safe by removing or restricting lethal means.
Held by the person, shared as they decide, accessible in a crisis.

teach.body: Validation means communicating that the person's emotion makes sense in context, even when the behaviour is not helpful: 'Of course you feel overwhelmed after that phone call.' It is not agreeing with self-harm. Invalidating responses ('You're overreacting') tend to escalate distress. Validate first, then coach the skill.

The nurse stays with Chloe, speaks calmly and validates: 'This urge feels unbearable right now.' She checks Chloe's immediate safety and asks what her safety plan and DBT skills card suggest. Because Chloe is highly aroused, she starts with TIPP: cold water on the face and paced breathing together. Once calmer, they use distraction and self-soothing. The nurse records the episode, the skills used and the outcome, and passes it to Chloe's DBT therapist.

teach.text: Distress tolerance is NOT about removing the emotion or solving the problem tonight; it is about getting through the crisis without making it worse. And do not reach for PRN sedation as 'treatment' for self-harm urges: NICE says no drug treatment specifically to reduce self-harm (NG225 1.11.10).

items: DBT modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness.
CG78: consider comprehensive DBT for women with BPD where reducing self-harm is a priority; NG225: DBT-A for adolescents.
Crisis skills: TIPP, distraction, self-soothing, urge surfing; validate first.
Safety plans are made with, held by and shared as decided by the person.

summary: You can now describe the four DBT modules and who NICE recommends DBT for. You can also coach someone through an urge with TIPP, distraction and self-soothing, using validation and a collaborative safety plan.

A.q: Which is one of the four skill modules of dialectical behaviour therapy?
options: Exposure and response prevention
Interpersonal effectiveness
Cognitive restructuring
Eye movement desensitisation
A.why: DBT's four modules are mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness.

whyNot.0: ERP is a CBT technique for OCD.
whyNot.2: Cognitive restructuring is a core CBT technique, not a DBT module.

A.q: For which group does NICE CG78 suggest considering a comprehensive DBT programme?
options: Men with antisocial personality disorder in prison
Adults with first-episode psychosis
Women with BPD where reducing self-harm is a priority
Older adults with generalised anxiety and panic disorder
A.why: CG78: for women with borderline personality disorder for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority, consider a comprehensive DBT programme.

whyNot.0: CG78's DBT recommendation is for women with BPD.
whyNot.1: Psychosis is treated with CBTp and family intervention (CG178).
whyNot.3: GAD is treated with CBT or applied relaxation (CG113).

A.q: In the DBT skill TIPP, what does the 'T' stand for?
options: Temperature
Talking
Tolerance
Timing
A.why: TIPP: temperature (cold water), intense exercise, paced breathing, paired muscle relaxation; all change body arousal quickly.

whyNot.1: Talking is not part of TIPP.
whyNot.2: Tolerance is the module name, not the T in TIPP.
whyNot.3: Timing is not part of TIPP.

B.q: Ben, 15, has frequent episodes of self-harm and significant emotional dysregulation. Which therapy does NICE NG225 suggest considering?
options: DBT adapted for adolescents (DBT-A)
An SSRI to reduce self-harm
Psychodynamic therapy for 2 years
Single-session psychological debriefing
B.why: NG225 1.11.4: for children and young people with significant emotional dysregulation and frequent self-harm, consider DBT-A.

whyNot.1: NG225 1.11.10: no drug treatment specifically to reduce self-harm.
whyNot.2: This is not the NG225 recommendation for this group.
whyNot.3: Debriefing is not a treatment for self-harm.

B.q: A woman on the ward says, 'Everyone ignores me and I can't stand it.' Which nurse response is validating?
options: 'You're overreacting; we're all very busy.'
'Feeling unheard is really painful. Let's talk.'
'If you calm down, someone will see you later.'
'Other patients have bigger problems right now.'
B.why: Validation communicates that the emotion makes sense, without judging; it lowers distress and opens the way to skills coaching.

whyNot.0: This invalidates her feelings and is likely to escalate distress.
whyNot.3: Comparing her with others dismisses her experience.

B.q: Who should hold the safety plan developed with a person who has self-harmed, according to NICE NG225?
options: The GP, in the medical record
The care coordinator, in the team office
The nearest relative
The person themselves
B.why: NG225 1.11.8: the safety plan should be held by the person and shared with family, carers and professionals as the person decides.

whyNot.0: It may be shared with the GP, but the person holds it.
whyNot.1: The team may have a copy, but the person holds it.
whyNot.2: Sharing with family is the person's decision.

C.q: Chloe is pacing, breathing rapidly and says she cannot think straight because the urge to cut is so strong. Which skill should the nurse coach first?
options: Writing a full chain analysis of the trigger
Practising assertive requests to staff
TIPP: cold water on the face and paced breathing
Listing the long-term pros and cons of cutting
C.why: At very high arousal, thinking-based skills do not work; TIPP lowers physiological arousal quickly so other skills become possible.

whyNot.0: Chain analysis is done later, when calm, usually with the therapist.
whyNot.1: Interpersonal skills are not the first step in an acute urge.
whyNot.3: Pros and cons need clearer thinking than she has right now.

C.q: Sam is in ongoing treatment but cannot yet resist the urge to self-harm. The team discusses harm minimisation. Which approach fits NICE NG225?
options: Supply clean blades so that he can self-harm more safely
Agree strategies jointly as part of recovery-focused care
Offer harm minimisation as a standalone intervention
Avoid discussing wound care to prevent encouragement
C.why: NG225 1.11.11-1.11.12: consider harm minimisation in a spirit of hope, as part of an overall recovery approach, agreed collaboratively; discuss distraction, coping, self-care and wound aftercare.

whyNot.0: NG225 makes no recommendation on 'safer self-harm'.
whyNot.2: It should not be a standalone intervention.
whyNot.3: Wound hygiene and aftercare are named topics to discuss.

C.q: The day after a crisis, Chloe says the skills 'did nothing' because she still felt awful afterwards, although she did not cut. What is the best response?
options: Agree the skills failed and ask the doctor for PRN
Suggest she stops the DBT programme
Explain that she should have felt calm by the end
Highlight that she got through without cutting
C.why: The aim of distress tolerance is to survive a crisis without making it worse, not to remove painful feelings; praising her success reinforces skill use.

whyNot.0: The skills worked: she did not self-harm; PRN is not a self-harm treatment.
whyNot.1: Stopping DBT would remove an effective treatment.
whyNot.2: Distress tolerance does not promise calm feelings.

reteach.title: Survive the wave
reteach.question: What is distress tolerance actually for?

blocks.body: An urge is like a wave: it builds, peaks and falls. Distress tolerance skills do not stop the wave; they help the person stay afloat until it passes, without acting in ways that make things worse. Bring arousal down first (TIPP), then distract and self-soothe.

blocks.text: Still feeling bad but not self-harming is success.

explain.body: Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness. Acceptance plus change.

test.q: Which DBT module focuses on getting through a crisis without making it worse?
options: Emotion regulation
Interpersonal effectiveness
Mindfulness
Distress tolerance
test.why: Distress tolerance skills help a person survive crises without acting in ways that make things worse.

whyNot.0: Emotion regulation reduces vulnerability to emotions over time.
whyNot.1: Interpersonal effectiveness is about asking for needs and saying no.
whyNot.2: Mindfulness is awareness of the present moment, underpinning all modules.

explain.body: Temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, paired muscle relaxation: fast ways to lower physical arousal.

test.q: Why is paced breathing with a longer out-breath used in a crisis?
options: It lowers physical arousal quickly
It increases oxygen to stop panic
It distracts by counting to 100
It replaces the need for a safety plan
test.why: Slowing breathing, especially the out-breath, lowers physical arousal so the person can start to use other skills.

whyNot.1: The aim is calming arousal, not raising oxygen.
whyNot.2: Counting is a distraction skill, not the point of paced breathing.
whyNot.3: Skills sit within the safety plan, not instead of it.

explain.body: Triggers, warning signs, coping strategies, people and places, service contacts, removing lethal means; held by the person.

test.q: Which item does NICE NG225 include in the content of a safety plan?
options: A promise not to self-harm
Ways to restrict access to lethal means
A list of medicines to take in a crisis
A contract signed with the ward manager
test.why: NG225 1.11.7: safety plans include keeping the environment safe by collaboratively removing or restricting lethal means.

whyNot.0: No-harm promises are not part of the NG225 plan.
whyNot.2: No crisis medication list is specified.
whyNot.3: Safety plans are collaborative, not contracts.

explain.body: Communicate that the emotion makes sense, then coach skills. Invalidation escalates distress.

test.q: What does validation mean in DBT?
options: Agreeing that self-harm is a reasonable choice
Showing the emotion makes sense in context
Confirming the diagnosis to the person
Praising the person whatever they do
test.why: Validation communicates that the person's feelings are understandable in context, without endorsing harmful behaviour.

whyNot.0: Validation does not endorse harmful behaviour.
whyNot.3: It is targeted acknowledgement, not blanket praise.
